These results underscore our commitment to advancing assets with distinct scientific approaches aimed to address critical unmet patient needs." title: AbbVie Earnings Call Highlights Growth Amid Transition - The Globe and Mail
content: Abbvie ((ABBV)) has held its Q1 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call. AbbVie’s latest earnings call struck an upbeat tone, with management emphasizing strong commercial momentum, a broad-based sales beat and a raise to full-year guidance. Executives highlighted double-digit growth across key immunology and neuroscience franchises, robust pipeline progress and sizable U.S. manufacturing investments, while acknowledging ongoing HUMIRA erosion, oncology and aesthetics pressures, and higher R&D-related expenses. AbbVie posted adjusted EPS of $2.65, topping the guidance midpoint by $0.07, on total net revenues of $15.0 billion, roughly $300 million above expectations and up 12.4%. The company lifted full-year adjusted EPS guidance by $0.12 to a range of $14.08 to $14.28 and increased its full-year revenue outlook to about $67.3 billion, adding $300 million. Immunology remained the growth engine, delivering $7.3 billion in revenue, up about $1.0 billion year over year. Skyrizi generated $4.5 billion in sales, up 29.2% operationally, and Rinvoq contributed $2.1 billion, up 20.2%, as Skyrizi gains share in psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease with management targeting over 30% global IBD growth. Neuroscience revenues approached $2.9 billion, growing 24.3% operationally, underscoring AbbVie’s diversification beyond immunology. Vraylar delivered $905 million, rising 18.4%, while VYALEV reached $201 million with roughly 10% sequential growth, and the company is preparing for a potential U.S. launch of Parkinson’s therapy tavapadon later this year. Management underscored category leadership in key therapeutic and aesthetic segments, pointing to robust double-digit gains from Botox Therapeutic and its broader migraine portfolio. Botox Cosmetic sales reached $668 million, up 17%, while Skyrizi’s long-term data in psoriatic arthritis showed nearly 90% of patients without radiographic progression at five years and new labels for difficult psoriasis areas. The call highlighted pipeline momentum with several regulatory moves, including a U.S. filing for Rinvoq in alopecia areata. AbbVie also submitted Skyrizi’s subcutaneous induction for Crohn’s disease, with a decision expected later this year, and reported interim data on a Skyrizi plus ABBV-382 combination that suggested potentially transformational efficacy in Crohn’s. AbbVie touted early obesity-related signals from ABBV-295, a long-acting amylin analog, in a multiple-ascending-dose study. The candidate produced nearly 10% weight loss over 12 weeks in a predominantly male, nonobese group with favorable tolerability and a half-life of about 270 hours, supporting future development with every-other-week or monthly dosing. In oncology, the company is leaning on business development and combination strategies to refresh its portfolio, including a deal with Remagen for a PD-1/VEGF bispecific asset. AbbVie is pivoting its Temab-A program toward combination with bevacizumab in colorectal cancer after early data showed an objective response rate near 30% and disease control around 97%, with more details expected around ASCO. AbbVie detailed substantial capital plans as part of a broader U.S. R&D and investment pledge, including a $1.4 billion pharmaceutical campus in North Carolina. The company will also spend about $380 million on two plants in North Chicago to expand manufacturing capacity, reinforcing its confidence in long-term demand across key franchises. Profitability remained a focal point, with adjusted gross margin at 83.6% of sales and adjusted operating margin at 40.8% in the quarter, even after acquired in-process R&D. For the full year, AbbVie aims for an adjusted gross margin above 84% and an adjusted operating margin near 47.5%, framing the current quarter as a stepping stone toward higher margin levels. Financial flexibility improved as the company trimmed its adjusted net interest expense outlook to around $2.7 billion, about $100 million better than before. AbbVie reiterated its focus on record investment in the business, maintaining an active deal-making strategy and continuing to return cash to shareholders via a growing dividend. The long-expected decline of HUMIRA continued, with global sales down 40.3% operationally to $688 million as biosimilars pressure the franchise. Management framed this erosion as a known headwind within its transition plan, emphasizing that growth from Skyrizi, Rinvoq and newer assets is offsetting the loss of legacy HUMIRA revenue. Total oncology revenue slipped to $1.6 billion, down 3% operationally, reflecting specific portfolio challenges. IMBRUVICA sales dropped 24.7% due to pricing dynamics under the IRA and heightened competition, though this was partially balanced by Venclexta, which grew 9.7% to $770 million. Aesthetics delivered nearly $1.2 billion in revenue, up 5.1% operationally, but management acknowledged uneven performance within the segment. Juvederm sales declined 2.9% to $232 million amid continued dermal filler weakness in a tougher macro backdrop, compounded by a regulatory setback as one aesthetics application received a manufacturing-related FDA letter. The company also flagged some clinical disappointments, including ABBV-932 in bipolar depression, which failed to meet its primary endpoint overall despite a signal in bipolar I. Additionally, the Skyrizi plus lutikizumab combination did not show enough differentiation from Skyrizi alone and will be discontinued, underscoring AbbVie’s willingness to prune less compelling programs. Management noted that pricing remains a modest drag, with low-single-digit net price erosion expected across immunology for the year despite flat Skyrizi pricing in the first quarter. The quarter also included a modest inventory destocking effect, which the company framed as a temporary factor rather than a shift in underlying demand. Acquired in-process R&D spending weighed on reported earnings, producing a $0.41 unfavorable EPS impact in the quarter. This spending shaved roughly five percentage points from the adjusted operating margin ratio, and while current guidance excludes future IPR&D beyond the first quarter, management emphasized these costs as part of a deliberate investment strategy. Investors were reminded that some key programs remain in early stages or hinge on future trial designs and regulatory interactions, particularly within oncology. This leaves execution and timing risk around anticipated readouts and approvals, which could influence how quickly pipeline assets begin to contribute meaningfully to revenue and earnings. Management contrasted the current aesthetics environment with prior downturns, noting that while toxins like Botox historically proved resilient, fillers are seeing more pressure this time. This suggests a slower recovery for certain aesthetic lines, prompting a more measured outlook for that segment even as the broader business continues to grow. AbbVie’s updated outlook calls for full-year net revenues of about $67.3 billion and second-quarter revenues near $16.7 billion, including a modest currency benefit, with Skyrizi, Rinvoq and neuroscience each nudged higher by $100 million. The company targets an adjusted operating margin around 47.5%, gross margin above 84%, adjusted R&D near $9.7 billion, SG&A around $14.2 billion and reduced net interest expense of $2.7 billion, framing a trajectory of rising earnings power. AbbVie’s earnings call painted a picture of a company successfully navigating its post-HUMIRA transition, leveraging strong immunology and neuroscience growth to more than offset legacy headwinds. While oncology, aesthetics and certain pipeline setbacks remain watch points, the combination of a guidance raise, robust margin targets and visible capital deployment underpins a constructive outlook for investors focused on earnings durability and pipeline-driven upside. title: Dividend Healthcare Giants: Analyzing Pfizer (PFE), AbbVie (ABBV), and Medtronic (MDT) for 2026 - parameter.io
content: Income-focused investors are examining three healthcare sector heavyweights — Pfizer, AbbVie, and Medtronic — throughout 2026. While all three distribute dividends to shareholders, their operational strategies, risk profiles, and income characteristics differ substantially. The healthcare industry presents unique challenges. Pharmaceutical manufacturers must navigate patent cliffs, regulatory pricing constraints, and the inherent uncertainty of drug development. Medical device producers confront competitive pressures and fluctuating hospital capital budgets. Nevertheless, demographic shifts toward older populations and expanding global healthcare expenditures provide sustained tailwinds for the sector. Pfizer presently delivers the most attractive dividend yield among this trio, hovering near 6.7% on an annualized basis. The pharmaceutical giant announced its second-quarter 2026 distribution of $0.43 per share, scheduled for June 12 payment to stockholders registered by May 8. This upcoming payment represents Pfizer’s 350th uninterrupted quarterly dividend. The company’s total annual payout amounts to $1.72 per share. Such an elevated yield is uncommon among leading pharmaceutical enterprises. This typically indicates market skepticism regarding the company’s future expansion prospects — a reasonable concern considering Pfizer’s current position. The organization continues adapting to the dramatic revenue decline following its pandemic-driven peak. It confronts product lifecycle pressures and approaching patent losses on important medications. The enterprise requires a convincing transformation narrative for this generous yield to remain viable over extended periods. Investors prioritizing immediate income who accept this risk profile may find Pfizer compelling. Those seeking greater predictability might prefer exploring the alternative options. AbbVie announced a $1.73 quarterly dividend per share in February, distributed on May 15, 2026. Its yield ranges between 3.2% and 3.3%, trailing Pfizer’s but exceeding numerous large-capitalization competitors. AbbVie constructed its foundation upon Humira, which subsequently faced biosimilar competition following patent expiration. The critical question centered on whether emerging products could offset this revenue decline. Current results appear promising. The immunology treatments Skyrizi and Rinvoq have evolved into significant revenue contributors. AbbVie maintains additional presence across neuroscience, oncology, and aesthetic medicine. This diversified portfolio provides AbbVie with more compelling expansion prospects than typical high-yield securities. The primary risk involves operational execution — should newer medications underperform or pricing pressures intensify, financial performance could deteriorate. Medtronic represents an entirely different proposition. As a medical technology corporation rather than pharmaceutical manufacturer, its product portfolio spans cardiovascular therapies, diabetes management, surgical equipment, and neuroscience applications. This diversification distributes revenue across numerous therapeutic categories instead of concentrating on individual drugs. The company’s most distinguished characteristic is dividend reliability. Medtronic has increased its annual distribution for 48 consecutive years, securing inclusion in the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats index. Its current quarterly payment equals $0.71 per share. While the yield falls below Pfizer’s offering, the consistency record speaks volumes. The principal concern regarding Medtronic involves growth trajectory, as market participants question whether its innovation efforts can generate superior long-term returns. Among these three healthcare enterprises, each presents a unique investment thesis. Pfizer offers maximum current income alongside the greatest near-term business uncertainty. This is the point at which a drug loses its patent exclusivity and therefore becomes vulnerable to competition from any rival willing to reproduce the molecule. Earlier this decade, the web of patents protecting AbbVie's versatile blockbuster drug, Humira, began to expire, sparking concerns that it would make the company an also-ran. This didn't occur; in fact, AbbVie these days is thriving more than it did during the height of the drug's exclusivity and popularity. The combination of internal development and acquisitions has resulted in an impressive product lineup that includes 12(!) blockbusters, i.e., drugs that earn more than $1 billion in annual sales (including the still-strong Humira). With so many greenbacks flooding into its coffers, AbbVie has enough financial strength not only to fund its dividend but also to keep it growing. In fact, as the company was once part of habitual dividend raiser Abbott Laboratories, it qualifies as a Dividend King, the tiny clutch of U.S. stocks that have enacted dividend raises at least once per year for a minimum of 50 years straight. AbbVie's quarterly payout is $1.73 per share these days, and it was most recently raised in April. Medtronic is the largest pure-play medical device company on the scene, with annual revenue topping $33.5 billion. A sizable operator with considerable experience, the company offers a wide variety of goods crucial to the medical profession. These cover millions of patients and a great many practitioners. While Medtronic is a behemoth and therefore doesn't post high revenue growth, it's consistently profitable, with net margins that habitually land above 10%. As you can probably conclude, free cash flow has been far in the black; since 2020, on an annual basis, it's ranged from almost $4.6 billion to slightly under $6 billion. It should be no surprise, then, to learn that Medtronic's latest dividend raise was its 48th in a row, putting it within easy distance of Dividend King status. Meanwhile, given that the world's population is aging (and thus increasingly in need of medical care), Medtronic is well positioned for years of future growth and profitability.
